newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sees 5.5 pct growth in 1998, 9.5 pct CPI.
newsitem.headline: Poland sees 5.5 pct growth in 1998, 9.5 pct CPI.

text.p: The Polish government's economic council (KERM) on Monday approved a 1998 economic policy programme which assumes gross domestic product growth of up to 5.5 percent and annual inflation of around 9.5 percent.

"We predict that next year's growth should oscillate between five and 5.5 percent...and (year-on-year) inflation should reach between nine and 9.5 percent in December," Finance Minister Marek Belka said after the meeting of KERM which groups heads of economic ministries.
This year's growth is also expected to reach 5.5 percent while inflation is forecast to fall to below 13 percent in December from 14.6 percent in May.
Belka told a news conference the government would strive to curb the public debt by two points next year, from about 50 percent of GDP now.

He confirmed his earlier statements that under the policy scheme called "The 1998 Social and Economic Policy Assumptions", due to be debated on Tuesday by the whole cabinet, the budget deficit would be lowered to below two percent of GDP.
"(A higher deficit) would be unhealthy for the economy and... we would not be able to finance a greater deficit," Belka said.
He has earlier said the gap could not be bigger because the ministry has increasingly found it difficult to tap the domestic market.
This hurdle may force a reduction in the deficit in 1997 to below the originally planned 2.8 percent of GDP, even though the government did not want to go below this level, Belka said.
He stood by his earlier prediction that Poland's foreign trade deficit was likely to grow to up to $13 billion in 1997 from last year's $8.2 billion.
"If the deficit increases to this extent, it means that everything is under control. But if it grows further to $16 billion next year, this would indicate a threat to the economy," he said.

Some analysts have said that Czech-style economic troubles, with a swelling trade deficit, shrinking industrial production and a resulting currency devaluation, could be repeated in Poland. The government firmly denies this could happen.

Belka said that under the programme approved on Monday the priorities for 1998 were sustained growth, reform of the social security system, integration with the European Union and NATO, strengthening institutions on the capital market, building roads and upgrading the telecoms system.

Belka declined on comment on whether the central bank should slow the pace of the monthly zloty devaluation, now at one percent against a basket of foreign currencies. But he said he thought the pace was "quite substantial." -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
